title: EU imposes anti-dumping duties on cold-rolled steel from five origins as iron ore slides
intro: Brussels dominates today's edition. Several publishers report that the European Union has imposed anti-dumping duties on cold-rolled flat steel. Goodreturns names India, Japan, Taiwan, Turkiye and Vietnam as the origins. GMK Center reports duties of up to 27.9%, and bne IntelliNews puts the rate on Vietnamese steel at 16%. Shanghai Metals Market adds that the duties have started without retroactive collection. In China, BigMint reports that iron ore prices are at a near four-year low as weak steel prices curb mill buying. In the United States, Shanghai Metals Market reports that Nippon Steel is reviving a Pennsylvania mill with nearly 3 billion USD, while Nucor posts back-to-back shipment records and another hot-rolled coil price rise. Most items arrived as headlines only, so company-specific rates, volumes and price levels are largely unavailable.

marketOverview: Price signals today point in different directions, but the material contains few actual price levels. BigMint reports that iron ore in China has fallen to a near four-year low as weak steel prices curb mill buying, and a StoneX headline says China's steel slump has left iron ore bulls under pressure. Neither excerpt gives prices. In Europe, Shanghai Metals Market reports that hot-rolled coil is holding at highs, again without levels. In the United States, Yieh Corp. reports that Nucor raised its weekly HRC spot price by $15 per short ton. SteelRadar reports that Nucor Tubular Products has lifted pipe and tube prices by USD 100 per ton. Resulting price levels are not stated.

analysis: Analysis: Today's material suggests that trade defence is hardening on both sides of the Atlantic while Chinese demand weakness weighs on raw materials. The EU's cold-rolled duties, combined with the proposed CBAM extension to downstream products, could narrow the routes by which lower-priced Asian steel reaches European buyers. That may help explain why European HRC is reported to be holding at highs, though the excerpts do not establish a causal link. In the United States, Nucor's shipment records and repeated price rises, which the publisher connects to Section 232, point to a protected domestic market where producers retain pricing power. Nippon Steel's Pennsylvania investment fits that picture. A near four-year low in Chinese iron ore could ease input costs for blast-furnace producers elsewhere. It could also signal that surplus Chinese steel is searching for outlets, which would reinforce the protectionist trend. POSCO's position is notable: it is exposed to EU duties through Vietnam, faces labour unrest at home and is reviewing HBI supply in Australia. Readers should treat these links cautiously, given how thin the excerpts are.
